title: Unified Osculator Theorem
description: Merges the positive and negative osculator theorems into a single unified theorem with a signed osculator c in Z. The negative osculator case is derived as a corollary by substituting -c, and a dual osculator relationship theorem shows that the sum of positive and negative osculators is divisible by d.

overview.historicalContext: Divisibility rules using "osculators" (multipliers applied to the last digit) have roots in Martin Gardner's recreational mathematics and earlier work by V. Ramaswami Aiyar (1907). The positive osculator test ($d | n \iff d | (\lfloor n/10 \rfloor + c \cdot (n \bmod 10))$ when $10c \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$) and the negative variant ($10c \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$) have traditionally been treated as separate rules. The parent formalization (divisibility-truncation-general) proved both cases independently, raising the natural question: can they be unified? This proof shows the answer is yes — the negative case is the positive case with $c$ negated, since $d | (10c_{\text{neg}} + 1)$ implies $d | (10(-c_{\text{neg}}) - 1)$. The unification reveals a deeper structure: positive and negative osculators are not independent constructions but additive inverses under the same modular arithmetic. Osculators are closely related to modular multiplicative inverses: the positive osculator $c_+$ satisfies $10c_+ \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$, making $c_+$ the multiplicative inverse of 10 in $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$. The existence of such inverses (guaranteed by Bézout's identity when $\gcd(10, d) = 1$) connects these recreational divisibility tricks to core algebraic number theory and the extended Euclidean algorithm.
overview.problemStatement:
Can the positive and negative osculator theorems be merged into a single theorem with a signed osculator c in Z?

**Answer: YES.** The unified osculator theorem states: for any d coprime to 10 and any c in Z satisfying d | (10c - 1):

  d | n <-> d | (n/10 + c * (n%10))

The negative osculator case follows by substituting c = -c_neg, since d | (10*c_neg + 1) implies d | (10*(-c_neg) - 1).
overview.text: A 159-line unification of the osculator divisibility rules with 0 axioms and 0 sorries. The parent proof (divisibility-truncation-general) treats positive osculators ($10c \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$) and negative osculators ($10c \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$) as separate theorems. This proof merges them: the `unified_osculator_theorem` states $d \mid n \iff d \mid (\lfloor n/10 \rfloor + c \cdot (n \bmod 10))$ for any $c \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $d \mid (10c - 1)$, and the negative case follows by substituting $c \mapsto -c_{\text{neg}}$ since $d \mid (10c_{\text{neg}} + 1) \iff d \mid (10(-c_{\text{neg}}) - 1)$. The key algebraic identity is $10(\lfloor n/10 \rfloor + c(n \bmod 10)) = n + (10c-1)(n \bmod 10)$: when $d \mid (10c-1)$, the remainder term vanishes mod $d$, and `IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left` cancels the factor of 10. A bonus `dual_osculator_sum` theorem proves $d \mid (c_+ + c_-)$ via $10(c_+ + c_-) = (10c_+ - 1) + (10c_- + 1)$. Concrete instantiations verify $d = 7, 11, 13, 17, 19$ by `norm_num`.
overview.proofStrategy:
The unified theorem uses the same algebraic identity as the parent proof:

  10 * (n/10 + c*(n%10)) = n + (10c - 1)*(n%10)

When d | (10c - 1), the remainder term is divisible by d, and coprimality with 10 allows cancelling the factor of 10.

The negative case then follows by a simple sign flip: given d | (10*c_neg + 1), we show 10*(-c_neg) - 1 = -(10*c_neg + 1), so d | (10*(-c_neg) - 1). Applying the unified theorem with osculator -c_neg immediately yields the negative rule.

The dual osculator theorem observes that 10*c_pos - 1 + (10*c_neg + 1) = 10*(c_pos + c_neg), so d divides this sum, and coprimality gives d | (c_pos + c_neg).
keyInsights: The negative osculator case is not independent: it is the positive case with c negated.
Sign absorption: d | (10*c_neg + 1) iff d | (10*(-c_neg) - 1), reducing two theorems to one.
The dual osculator relationship (c_pos + c_neg divisible by d) follows from the sum of the two osculator conditions.
Lean's IsCoprime and linear_combination handle the algebraic manipulations cleanly.
All five classical divisibility rules (7, 11, 13, 17, 19) are recovered from the single unified theorem.
prerequisites: Coprimality and Bézout's identity ($\gcd(d, 10) = 1$ guarantees osculator existence)
Division algorithm and digit extraction ($n = 10 \lfloor n/10 \rfloor + n \bmod 10$)
Divisibility over $\mathbb{Z}$: linearity, transitivity, and coprime cancellation (`IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left`)

sections.title: The Unified Osculator Theorem
sections.summary: Single theorem: d | n <-> d | (n/10 + c*(n%10)) for any c with d | (10c - 1). Uses the identity 10*(n/10 + c*(n%10)) = n + (10c-1)*(n%10) and coprimality to transfer divisibility.
sections.mathContext: $d \mid n \iff d \mid (\lfloor n/10 \rfloor + c \cdot (n \bmod 10))$ whenever $\gcd(d, 10) = 1$ and $d \mid (10c - 1)$. Key identity: $10(\lfloor n/10 \rfloor + c(n \bmod 10)) = n + (10c-1)(n \bmod 10)$.

sections.title: Negative Osculator as Special Case
sections.summary: Derives the negative osculator rule from the unified theorem by substituting -c.
sections.mathContext: If $d \mid (10c_{\text{neg}} + 1)$, then $10(-c_{\text{neg}}) - 1 = -(10c_{\text{neg}} + 1)$, so $d \mid (10(-c_{\text{neg}}) - 1)$. Applying the unified theorem with osculator $-c_{\text{neg}}$ gives the negative rule as a one-line corollary.

sections.title: Recovering Both Specific Cases

sections.mathContext: Concrete examples: $d=7$ ($c_+ = 5$: $7 \mid n \iff 7 \mid (\lfloor n/10 \rfloor + 5(n \bmod 10))$; $c_- = -2$). $d=11$ ($c_+ = 10$; $c_- = -1$: the alternating-digit rule). $d=13$ ($c_+ = 4$; $c_- = -9$).

crossReferences.description: Unifies the separate positive and negative osculator theorems from the parent proof into a single theorem with signed osculator $c \in \mathbb{Z}$, reducing two theorems to one
Bézout's identity guarantees the existence of the osculator $c$: since $\gcd(10, d) = 1$, there exist $s, t$ with $10s + dt = 1$, giving $c = s$ as the multiplicative inverse of 10 mod $d$

Unique prime factorization underpins the coprimality condition $\gcd(d, 10) = 1$, which is necessary for the osculator to exist. Divisors sharing factors with 10 (i.e., multiples of 2 or 5) require the last-$k$-digits framework instead

The digit-sum rule for divisibility by 3 (and 9) is the simplest osculator rule: since $10 \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, the osculator $c = 1$ gives $3 \mid n \iff 3 \mid (\lfloor n/10 \rfloor + 1 \cdot (n \bmod 10))$, which iterates to the digit sum

Euler's totient function $\varphi(d)$ counts invertible elements in $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$. The osculator $c$ is the multiplicative inverse of 10 mod $d$, which exists iff $\gcd(10, d) = 1$ — a condition guaranteed by Euler's theorem: $10^{\varphi(d)} \equiv 1 \pmod{d}$

CRT provides an alternative approach to osculator construction: for composite $d = d_1 d_2$ with $\gcd(d_1, d_2) = 1$, the osculator can be computed via the Chinese Remainder Theorem from the osculators of $d_1$ and $d_2$

conclusion.summary: The positive and negative osculator theorems are successfully unified into a single theorem. The key insight is that the negative osculator with parameter c_neg is equivalent to the positive osculator with parameter -c_neg. This reduces the two-theorem framework to a single unified osculator theorem, with the negative case as a one-line corollary. Additionally, the dual osculator sum theorem reveals a structural relationship between the two osculator constants.
conclusion.implications:
This unification:
- **Simplifies the framework**: One theorem instead of two, with the negative case as a corollary
- **Reveals structure**: The dual osculator sum theorem shows c_pos + c_neg is always a multiple of d
- **Confirms universality**: Every divisor coprime to 10 has exactly one osculator up to sign
- **Enables extensions**: The single-theorem framework is easier to generalize to other bases
openQuestions: Can this be extended to divisors that share factors with 10 by combining with the last-k-digits framework?
What is the relationship between the osculator and the continued fraction expansion of 1/d?
Can multi-digit truncation (removing k digits at a time) be unified similarly?
